Stiff-person syndrome: Commonly mistaken for hysterical
paralysis
article info
Keywords:
Stiff-person syndrome
Anti-GAD antibodies
Hysterical paralysis
Conversion disorder
Dear Sir
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neurologic disease with
dramatic manifestations. The condition is thought to have an
autoimmune etiology. Associated neuropsychiatric symptoms of
SPS cause it to be mistaken for hysterical paralysis, a conversion dis-
order which presents with voluntary motor deﬁcits that suggest a
neurological or general medical condition. However, after thorough
evaluation, the symptoms are found to be unrelated to a physical
cause [1].
Important differences between the presentation of SPS and hys-
terical paralysis must be identiﬁed to initiate appropriate therapy.
SPS generally has a progressive course, while conversion disorders
rarely persist after 1 year [2]. Additionally, the presence of autoan-
tibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) is commonly
used as a diagnostic marker for SPS [3]. Following diagnosis with
SPS, a patient may be treated with intravenous immunoglobulin
(IVIg) therapy, baclofen, and benzodiazepines [4].
We present a case of a 29-year-old black woman who pre-
sented with progressive rigidity of the lower extremities that
had occurred over the course of a year. She was previously diag-
nosed with hysterical paralysis of the lower extremities. Her
rigidity worsened during several months of observation, eventu-
ally encompassing her trunk, neck and upper extremities. Tests
measuring creatine kinase, toxins, and heavy metals yielded neg-
ative results. Physical exam revealed 1+ reﬂexes throughout, and
gross rigidity with slight lordosis. Bladder and bowel functions
were normal. Results of multiple imaging studies of the brain and
lower spine were negative. A psychiatric consultation concluded
that there was little evidence supporting a functional origin for her
symptoms.
At this point, a reevaluation of her symptoms led to a suspected
case of SPS. A test measuring GAD antibodies was elevated at
62 U/ml (normal: <1). The diagnosis was conﬁrmed by neurology
consult. The patient began treatment with baclofen, diazepam and
bi-annual IVIg therapy. Over several months, the patient showed
marked improvement.
The rarity of SPS contributes to its common misdiagnosis as a func-
tional disorder. On the other hand, many case studies of patients
with SPS have been released recently, some including groups of
over 20 patients [5]. For this reason, SPS is an important diagnostic
consideration for a patient thought to have hysterical paralysis.
References
[1] Tinsley JA, Barth EM, Black JL, et al. Psychiatric consultations in stiff-man syn-
drome. J Clin Psychiatry 1997;58:444–9.

[2] Letonoff EJ, Williams TR, Sidhu KS. Hysterical paralysis: a report of three cases
and a review of the literature. Spine 2002;27(20):E441–445.
[3] Chang T, Lang B. GAD antibodies in stiff-person syndrome. Neurology
2004;63:1999.
[4] Dalakas MC, Fujii M, Li M, et al. High-dose intravenous immune globulin for

[5] Barker RA, Revesz T, Thom M, et al. Review of 23 patients affected by the stiff

Stiff-person syndrome in a female patient with type 1 diabetes,
dermatitis herpetiformis, celiac disease, microcytic anemia and
copper deﬁciency
Just a coincidence or an additional shared pathophysiological
mechanism?
Sir,
We have read with great interest a recent paper published in your
journal of a patient suffering from stiff-person syndrome (SPS), type
1 diabetes mellitus (DM), dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) and celiac
disease (CD). We want to report a patient with the same clinical
presentation, also diagnosed with microcytic anemia with normal
iron level and decreased copper level in serum [1].
Our patient with SPS was admitted because of pain and spasms
in back and right leg. The serum GAD IgG titer was 1548 /H9262g/mL.
She had been suffering from type 1 DM and from frequent diar-

Letter to the Editor / Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery 1 1 1 (2009) 643–646 645
rhea. The anti-endomysial IgA and anti-tissue transglutaminase
IgA antibodies were positive, small intestinal biopsy was done and
the diagnosis of celiac disease was conﬁrmed. Her skin rash was
examined and skin biopsy indicated the diagnosis of dermatitis
herpetiformis. Laboratory tests showed microcytic anemia with
normal iron and serum ferritin levels, and a decreased copper
level. Menkes disease was excluded, plasma ceruloplasmin level
and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal.
Both patients with SPS reported had antibodies against glutamic
decarboxylase [1]. However, comorbidity of SPS with the same
group of other autoimmune diseases in these two cases gives rise to
the possibility that, beside the autoimmune mechanism, one some
other additional pathophysiologic mechanism may be involved.
Henri-Bhargava et al. [2] describe a patient with leg stiffness, gait
unsteadiness and celiac disease presenting with dermatitis herpeti-
formis due to vitamin E and copper deﬁciencies. Copper is a cofactor
for numerous coenzymes and metalloproteins essential for normal
neurologic function and induces apoptosis via p53 dependent and
independent pathways. Thus, disorders of apoptosis may play a crit-
ical role in some of the most debilitating metal-induced afﬂictions
including neurotoxicity and autoimmunity [3,4].
The low level of serum copper in our patient opens a question of
the role of copper and possibly other trace elements in the develop-
ment of these autoimmune diseases. We cannot say with any degree
of certainty whether a signiﬁcant decrease in copper serum levels
plays a role in the development of numerous autoimmune diseases
in our patient, but an inadequate status of copper and other trace
elements may play a role in the processes of neurodegeneration
and autoimmunity. Therefore, it may be advisable to determine the
levels of trace elements in such patients with complex neurologic
autoimmune syndromes.
References
[1] O’ Sullivan EP, Behan LA, King TFJ, Hardiman O, Smith D. A case od stiff-person
syndrome, type 1 diabetes, celiac disease and dermatitis herpetiformis. Clin
Neurol Neurosurg 2009;1 1 1(4):384–6.
[2] Henri-Bhargava A, Melmed C, Glikstein R, Schipper HM. Neurologic impair-
ment due to vitamin E and copper deﬁciencies in celiac disease. Neurology
2008;71(1 1):860–1.
[3] Cerimagic D, Bilic E. Stiff-person syndrome ﬁrst manifesting in pregnancy.
Gynecol Obstet Invest 2008;67(2):134–6.
[4] Rana SV. Metals and apoptosis: recent developments. J Trace Elem Med Biol
2008;22(4):262–84.
